hook: A weather report says the average temperature yesterday was 19 °C. It was never "19 for the whole day"; it was colder at dawn and warmer at three. The average is the one steady temperature that would have built up the same total. For a function, that total is an integral, and the average value is the integral divided by the length of the interval.

prereq.why: Change in output over change in input: the slope of the secant line.

figure.caption: $f(x) = 6x - x^2$ on $[0, 6]$: the area under $f$ is 36, the same as a $6 \times 6$ rectangle, so the average value is 6.

chain.cause: $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ is the signed area, or the total accumulated
chain.effect: spread it evenly over the interval to get one steady height
$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{b - a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$, in the units of $f$
$f$ takes its average value at some $c$ in $[a, b]$ (between its minimum and maximum, by the Intermediate Value Theorem)
$\frac{1}{b - a}\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$, the average rate of change of $f$

ideas: Average value of $f$ on $[a, b]$: $\frac{1}{b - a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$. The integrand is $f$ itself.
Average value is a height, in the units of $f$. Average rate of change, $\frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$, is a slope, in units of $f$ per unit of $x$.
Areas below the axis count as negative, exactly as in the integral.
If $f$ is continuous, some $c$ in $[a, b]$ has $f(c) = f_{\text{avg}}$.
From a graph use geometry for the integral; from a table use a Riemann or trapezoidal sum; from a formula use the Fundamental Theorem or a calculator.

misconception.wrong: The average value of $f$ on $[0, 8]$ is $\frac{f(0) + f(8)}{2}$, or $\frac{f(8) - f(0)}{8}$.
misconception.right: The first averages two values and ignores the rest; the second is the average rate of change. The average value uses every value: $\frac{1}{8}\int_0^8 f(x)\,dx$.

summary: The average value of $f$ on $[a, b]$ is $\frac{1}{b - a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$, the height of the equal-area rectangle, in the units of $f$. A continuous $f$ reaches it somewhere on the interval. Do not confuse it with the average rate of change $\frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$, which is the average value of $f'$.
